notes: Slot 4 = Communist Party of Kirghizia (Usubaliyev). Usubaliyev's Naryn network in 13, southern Osh/Jalal-Abad elites in 14, Aitmatov circle ('Ak keme', after The White Ship, 1970) in 2, Manas tradition (Karalaev) in 1, SADUM qaziyat in 10, 8th Guards 'Panfilov' MRD (Frunze) in 22, Rahman Qul's Afghan Pamir Kyrgyz in 23. MD sprites show post-1991 organizations, so icons are null.

0.name: Radio Liberty Kyrgyz Service
0.text:
The Radio Liberty Kyrgyz Service broadcasts from Munich under the American Committee for Liberation, a body quietly financed by the CIA. Its small staff of Kyrgyz émigrés, most of them former Red Army prisoners of war who refused to return home, read news, religious talks and banned literature into a jammed frequency aimed at Frunze and Osh.

It champions a Kyrgyzstan freed from Soviet rule and tied to the West, and its émigré circle admires strong anti-communist governments in Ankara and Tehran more than parliamentary niceties. Its leverage is the shortwave radio: few listen openly, but every party official knows that the voice from Munich is heard in the mountain villages.

1.name: Manas korgoochulary
1.text:
The Defenders of Manas are the scholars, teachers and epic singers who rescued the Manas epic after it was denounced as feudal in 1952. Their living symbol in 1970 is the great manaschi Sayakbay Karalaev, whose recitations fill concert halls and whose versions are being recorded by the Academy of Sciences.

They stand for continuity: the epic, the clan genealogy, respect for elders and the Kyrgyz language as the soul of the nation. They avoid open politics and accept Soviet power, but distrust Russification and the uprooting of nomadic culture. Their leverage is moral authority over a people for whom Manas is still scripture, history and law combined.

2.name: Ak keme
2.text:
The White Ship is the circle of writers, film-makers and young scholars around Chingiz Aitmatov, the Lenin Prize laureate whose novella of that name appears in the Moscow journal Novy Mir in 1970. They are the Kyrgyz face of the Thaw, admired across the Union and protected by Aitmatov's fame.

They stand for conscience over dogma: freedom of artistic expression, truth about the past, protection of nature and of national memory against careerist officials. They remain inside the Soviet system and avoid any link to the West. Their leverage is prestige: Aitmatov's books sell in millions, his films are seen everywhere and even the Central Committee hesitates to attack him.

3.name: Kosyginchiler
3.text:
The Kosygin Reformers are economists, planners and enterprise directors in Frunze who embraced the economic reform launched by Alexei Kosygin in 1965, with its enterprise autonomy, profit indicators and material incentives. By 1970 the reform is stalling in Moscow, but its supporters still run factories and departments of the Kirghiz Gosplan.

They want managers freed from petty planning, wages tied to productivity, consumer goods for workers and more investment in light industry and services. They remain loyal socialists and support the USSR's foreign line, but admire Hungarian and Yugoslav experiments. Their leverage lies in measurable results and in allies within the State Planning Committee in Moscow.

4.name: Kyrgyzstan Kommunisttik Partiyasy
4.text:
The Communist Party of Kirghizia is the republican branch of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union and the only legal party of the Kirghiz SSR. Since 1961 it has been led by First Secretary Turdakun Usubaliyev, an energetic and loyal Brezhnev-era leader who never misses a chance to praise Moscow.

The party drives industrialisation, the Toktogul hydropower scheme, sheep breeding and the education of a Kyrgyz professional class, while firmly suppressing anything that smells of nationalism. It backs the USSR against both the United States and China across the Tian Shan. Its power rests on the nomenklatura, the obkoms of Osh, Naryn and Issyk-Kul, and Usubaliyev's standing in Moscow.

5.name: Toktogul GES kuruluschulary
5.text:
The Toktogul Dam Builders are the young Komsomol volunteers, engineers and labourers raising the giant hydroelectric dam in the Naryn gorge, the largest construction site in the republic. They live in barracks and settlements cut off by the mountains, and their brigades are a world of their own.

They are radical egalitarians: they want the brigades to run the work, equal pay for equal toil, an end to privileges for managers and the original enthusiasm of the revolution restored. They despise bureaucrats more than any foreign power. Their leverage is that the dam, vital for all of Central Asia's water and power, depends on their morale.

6.name: Eski gvardiya
6.text:
The Old Guard gathers the Stalin-era cadres of the Kirghiz party, police and procuracy, Russian and Kyrgyz alike, who rose during the purges and the war and were sidelined under Khrushchev. Since 1964 they have regained confidence and sit in district committees, the security organs and the veterans' councils of Frunze.

They demand discipline, a restored cult of Stalin's achievements, harsh treatment of nationalists and believers, and total obedience to Moscow. They regard Aitmatov's liberals and the clan networks with equal contempt and see China and America as mortal enemies. Their leverage is experience in repression, ties to Moscow's conservatives and the authority of the war generation.

7.name: Kyrgyz SSRinin Mamlekettik Koopsuzduk Komiteti
7.text:
The KGB of the Kirghiz SSR is the republican arm of the Committee for State Security, answering to Yuri Andropov in Moscow. Since the Sino-Soviet clashes of 1969 its frontier work along the Tian Shan has grown sharply, and it watches over the closed torpedo range on Lake Issyk-Kul and the uranium sites of the republic.

It stands for vigilance and control: informers in every institute, pressure on unregistered mullahs, surveillance of Uyghur and Dungan refugees and of anyone in contact with the West. Loyal first to Moscow, it keeps files on the local elite as well. Its leverage is secrecy, the border troops and the fear its name inspires.

8.name: Pomiriyoni Osh
8.text:
The Pamiris of Osh are Ismaili Shia drivers, traders, students and workers from Gorno-Badakhshan who live in Osh, the northern terminus of the Pamir Highway that links the Fergana Valley with Khorog. In 1970 they form a small but close-knit community among the Uzbek and Kyrgyz majority of the south.

They follow the Aga Khan as their imam and practise a tolerant, inward faith that values education and hard work. They seek only the freedom to meet, help one another and keep in touch with Badakhshan. They avoid confrontation with the state. Their leverage lies in the highway trade, mutual aid and contacts that stretch across the Pamirs.

9.name: Mähärräm camaatı
9.text:
The Muharram Congregation brings together the Azerbaijani and Kurdish Shia families deported to the Chuy and Talas valleys from the Caucasian frontier in 1937 and during the war. In 1970 a few elderly mullahs lead secret mourning rites for Imam Husayn in private homes, far from any registered mosque.

They believe the community must be guided by learned clerics, not by the state or by the Sunni muftiate, and they condemn Soviet atheism and the corruption of morals alike. They have no foreign patron but revere the shrines of Iraq and Iran. Their leverage is the discipline of a small, persecuted community and its stubborn devotion.

10.name: Kyrgyzstan musulmandarynyn kaziyaty
10.text:
The Qaziate of Kirghizia is the republican office of the Spiritual Administration of the Muslims of Central Asia and Kazakhstan, the state-recognised muftiate headed in Tashkent by Mufti Ziyauddin Babakhanov. From Frunze it supervises the handful of registered mosques in the republic, most of them in Osh and the Fergana Valley.

It preaches a loyal, scholarly Hanafi Islam that accepts the Soviet order, condemns shrine worship and unlicensed mullahs, and praises Soviet peace policy before foreign guests. It works under the eye of the Council for Religious Affairs. Its leverage is legitimacy: the only legal imams, the right to issue fatwas and the trust of older believers.

11.name: Osh hujralary
11.text:
The Hujras of Osh are clandestine study cells in the old Uzbek quarters of Osh and Jalal-Abad, linked to the underground teaching network of the Fergana Valley and to the circle of Muhammadjan Hindustani in Dushanbe. Young pupils memorise the Quran and Arabic grammar in back rooms, beyond the reach of the official muftiate.

The most radical among them reject their teachers' quietism, call the Soviet state infidel rule and dream of an Islamic order governed by sharia across Central Asia. They are hostile to Moscow and to the West alike. Their leverage is secrecy, devotion and the deep piety of the southern mahallas around the sacred Sulayman mountain.

12.name: Dungan jamaaty
12.text:
The Dungan Community gathers the Chinese-speaking Hui Muslims of the Chuy Valley, descendants of those who fled the Qing armies with Bai Yanhu in 1877-1878. In villages such as Aleksandrovka and Milyanfan they run model kolkhozes and keep mosques, Arabic teaching and family law alive more openly than their neighbours.

They favour a pious but practical Islam built on community self-help, education, commerce and moral discipline, and they seek respect for their faith rather than power. They are loyal to the Soviet state, which protects them from China. Their leverage lies in prosperous farms, close-knit clans and the reputation of Dungan farmers across the republic.

13.name: Naryn tobu
13.text:
The Naryn Group is the patronage network around First Secretary Turdakun Usubaliyev, a native of the Naryn region, and the northern clans who dominate the party apparatus and ministries in Frunze. Since 1961 Usubaliyev has placed relatives, classmates and fellow highlanders in key posts across the republic.

It pursues stability and the accumulation of local power: steady plan fulfilment for Moscow, generous resources for the north and silence about clan politics. Its loyalty to the Soviet line is total in public and pragmatic in private. Its leverage is control of appointments, housing and investment, and Usubaliyev's close relationship with Leonid Brezhnev.

14.name: Tüshtük
14.text:
The South is the bloc of kolkhoz chairmen, district officials and village elders of Osh and Jalal-Abad provinces, the populous, cotton-growing half of the republic that feels shut out of power by northerners in Frunze. Kyrgyz and Uzbek notables there share a world of bazaars, mosques, lineages and patronage.

They defend traditional family life, respect for elders and a fair share of posts and investment for the south. They are loyal to Soviet rule in form but govern by custom in practice, and have no interest in foreign blocs. Their leverage is numbers, the cotton harvest and the ability to deliver or withhold the south's cooperation.

15.name: Khaydarkanskiy rtutnyy kombinat
15.text:
The Khaidarkan Mercury Combine in the southern Alay foothills is the Soviet Union's main mercury producer and the flagship of Kirghizia's non-ferrous industry, alongside the Kadamjai antimony works and the uranium mills of Kara-Balta. Its directors answer to all-Union ministries in Moscow rather than to Frunze.

The mining managers want investment, priority supplies, closed towns with good shops and freedom from local interference. They see themselves as the real economic elite of the republic and care little for ideology. Their leverage is strategic metals for the defence industry, budgets controlled from Moscow and the jobs on which whole mountain towns depend.

16.name: Osh jaymasy
16.text:
The Osh Bazaar stands for the traders of the great Jayma market of Osh, one of the oldest bazaars of the Silk Road, and the private dealers of the Fergana Valley who supply what the state shops cannot. Fruit, livestock, carpets, smuggled goods and deficit spare parts move through networks of kin and bribes.

They want freedom to trade, to own and to profit, and an end to raids by the economic police. They care little about Moscow's politics and admire Western goods more than Western ideas. Their leverage is economic: the whole south, and many officials, live partly from the bazaar.

17.name: Ysyk-Köl mamlekettik korugu
17.text:
The Issyk-Kul State Nature Reserve was created in 1948 to protect the shores and wetlands of the great mountain lake, a refuge for migrating birds. Its biologists, together with scientists in Przhevalsk and Frunze, form the core of the republic's conservation movement in 1970.

They warn against falling water levels caused by irrigation, pollution from new resorts and the secret naval torpedo range on the lake, and they call for protection of snow leopards and juniper forests. They work within the Soviet system and avoid open protest. Their leverage is scientific authority and the love of all Kyrgyz for Issyk-Kul.

18.name: Malchylar
18.text:
The Herders are the shepherds, chabans and sovkhoz workers of the high pastures, the backbone of the republic's ten million sheep and its rural Kyrgyz majority. In 1970 they live in collective farms whose plans reward wool and meat but leave mountain families with poor schools, roads and clinics.

They want collective farming that serves the herders: higher procurement prices, more machinery, winter shelters, social services in remote valleys and respect for seasonal migration. They are loyal to Soviet socialism and indifferent to foreign blocs. Their leverage is that the republic's main export to the Union, wool and meat, depends entirely on their labour.

19.name: Abdrakhmanovchular
19.text:
Abdrakhmanov's Heirs are intellectuals and officials who honour Yusup Abdrakhmanov, the head of the Kirghiz government in 1927-1933, who defended Kyrgyz interests against Moscow and was shot in 1938. Rehabilitated in 1958, his memory inspires historians, teachers and younger party members in Frunze.

They are convinced communists who want a truly sovereign Kyrgyz socialist republic: native cadres, Kyrgyz-language education, development of the mountains rather than extraction, and an honest history of collectivisation. They reject both capitalism and Russian chauvinism. Their leverage lies in the Academy of Sciences, the universities and the quiet sympathy of many Kyrgyz officials.

20.name: Ürkün
20.text:
Ürkün, the exodus, is the name the Kyrgyz give to the uprising of 1916 against wartime labour conscription and the flight across the Tian Shan into China, in which a large part of the northern Kyrgyz perished. In 1970 the subject is almost taboo, but the memory is kept alive in villages, songs and family stories.

The populist mood it feeds holds that the land belongs to the Kyrgyz, that Russian settlers took the best valleys and that local people must come first in jobs, housing and schools. It is suspicious of both Moscow and outsiders. Its leverage is grievance, the countryside and young men angry at their place in the cities.

21.name: Korboshular
21.text:
The Kurbashis are the last veterans and descendants of the Basmachi commanders who fought Soviet power in the Alay and Fergana mountains until the early 1930s, together with their kinsmen who fled to Afghanistan, China and Turkey. In 1970 they are old men and secret family traditions, watched by the KGB.

Their ideal is a militarised Turkic nation purged of Russians and communists, ruled by warrior chiefs and the law of the sword. Fiercely anti-Soviet, they hope for any foreign war that might weaken Moscow. Their leverage is a legend of mountain resistance and blood ties to émigré communities across the border.

22.name: 8-ya gvardeyskaya motostrelkovaya diviziya
22.text:
The 8th Guards Motor Rifle Division, named after General Ivan Panfilov, descends from the division raised in Alma-Ata and Frunze in 1941 that won fame defending Moscow. Since 1967 it has been stationed in Frunze, and after the 1969 border clashes it forms the core of the Central Asian Military District's defences against China.

Its officers demand absolute priority for the frontier, discipline over clan politics and modern equipment for a possible war in the Tian Shan. They are loyal to the Soviet leadership but scornful of civilian weakness. Their leverage is force, the Panfilov legend that every Kyrgyz schoolchild learns, and Moscow's fear of China.

23.name: Kichi Pamir
23.text:
The Kyrgyz of the Little Pamir are the nomads of the Afghan Wakhan, many descended from families who fled Soviet collectivisation and the Basmachi wars, ruled by their khan Haji Rahman Qul. On 1 January 1970 they live under the protection of the Afghan king, a few days' ride from the Soviet border.

Rahman Qul governs as a patriarchal khan, owning most of the herds and judging his people by custom and Islamic law. He is fiercely anti-communist and sees himself as the guardian of free Kyrgyz life. His leverage lies in the legitimacy of the last independent Kyrgyz ruler and in the dream of a khanate restored in the mountains.
